To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

• The probability of a filler-gap dependency occurring in a syntactically-embedded memory element is very low, and that this low probability can be explained by the low probability of a filler- gap dependency co-occurring with a syntactically-nested con- stituent.

• The syntactic contiguities of Schuler et. al. (2012) are a sufficient condition for the existence of a probabilistic model of working memory that can reconstruct syntactic trees with a coverage of over 99.99% of the sentences of the Penn Treebank WSJ corpus.
(a) a model with four memory elements has the capa- city to reconstruct phrase structure for over 99% of sentences in a large corpus, and (b) this capacity is not increased by adding memory elements.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether sentence comprehension takes place in a general- purpose working memory, and if so, what are the memory re- quirements of this process?

the question of whether comprehension takes place in a general purpose working memory store using a simple notion (syntact- ically-contiguous incomplete constituents) of incomplete con- stituent states as memory elements, or in a dedicated syntac- tic parser.
the question of whether the working memory requirements of sentence comprehension can be predicted from the structure of the sentences being processed.

The main takeaway from our work is that
a simple model of working memory requirements based on a syntactic notion of incomplete constituents is able to explain the comprehensibility of a large corpus of natural language text.

, to the extent that a general-purpose working store can be used for sentence comprehension, it is sufficient to retain incomplete syntactic constituents in this store, and that this is compatible with Cowan’s (2001) estimate of working memory capacity.
, in the absence of non-structural information, a simple model of syntactic structure can reconstruct phrase structures for almost all the sentences in a corpus.
